VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01714

Long before the Seal of the Prophets, earlier prophets brought humanity the same message. They called people to the same religion of love for the divine Face revealed to each of them. Acceptance of that love was their paradise; refusal was their hell. In a long conversation with his disciple Mufaddal, the Sixth Imam explains that the Imam is the one who separates those destined for paradise from those destined for hell. He does not even have to judge them: their love or hatred of the Imam already constitutes their paradise or hell.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01715

In this sense, Ridwan, the angel of paradise, and Malik, the guardian of hell, may be understood as proceeding from the Imam's command. It has been this way since the first prophetic missions, and will remain so throughout the cycle of walayat. “The Shiites find salvation through an act of love for their Imam.” This saying brings to mind, in certain respects, the idea of salvation in Pure Land Buddhism.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01716

As he introduces his disciple to the mystery of this universal religion of love, encompassing all believers, Imam Ja'far ends with a warning: “Mufaddal, keep all this carefully. It is a treasure of secret, hidden knowledge. Show it only to those worthy of receiving it.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01717

Why must the Treasure remain hidden? Because only someone who can see from a much wider spiritual horizon is ready for it. We have already approached that horizon in the mystery of the primordial Muhammadan Reality and the existence of pure spiritual beings before their earthly lives. There, in the world of Spirit, everything takes place before earthly creatures and individual human histories come into being. Every prophet, in this understanding, proclaimed the same eternal Imam, the one who is, as we saw in Chapter V, the “place” where the mission and message of the prophets become manifest. This is what Imam Ja'far is trying to explain.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01718

At first Mufaddal cannot understand. How could prophets who lived earlier have loved the Imam? How could their followers or opponents have found paradise or hell in loving or rejecting him? Ja'far answers: “Do you not know that God Most High sent his Messenger—that is, a Spirit, the prophetic Word—to the prophets, who were themselves spirits created two thousand years before the creation of earthly beings? Do you not know that this Spirit called them to the threefold declaration of faith?”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01719

Once again, Shiite spiritual philosophy places sacred history within a reality beyond historical time, where what exists before earthly life and what exists after it are present together. The number used to express the precedence of the spiritual world can vary; it measures a different kind of time, a “subtle time.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01720

The distinction between before and after, and the rule that time cannot run backwards, belong to the order of events in our ordinary historical time—the “dense” or “opaque” time (zaman kathif). They do not apply in the same way to events that remain present together in the world of Spirit. In the Imam's explanation there is no mistaken chronology, nor an impossible placing of one historical event before another. There is a complete togetherness of events that we can understand only from the spiritual horizon opened by the teaching about the Imam.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01721

This same understanding lies behind the idea of a single spiritual body formed by everyone who has ever followed, or now follows, this eternal religion of walayat. The source of that love is God himself, revealing himself through those who are the objects of his love. And because God loves them, they possess a special claim—one that was invoked even before their earthly lifetimes. This is already an answer to Mufaddal's question.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01722

In a tradition about the Prophet's ascent to heaven, at the moment when he was “at the distance of two bows” mentioned in the Surah of the Star (53:9), the Prophet tells Ali that he heard God say: “I wrote your Name and his Name upon my Throne before I created any creatures, out of my love for you both. Whoever loves you and takes you as friends is counted among those brought near to Me. Whoever rejects your walayat and turns away from you is counted among the ungodly who break faith.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01723

This tradition has several versions and has been pondered endlessly in Shiism. It points to the very source of walayat: God's own love, the love of the Hidden Treasure for the primordial Light that comes from it and reveals it to created beings. That divine love, in turn, is the source of the love (walayat and mahabbat) that believers feel for the Fourteen primordial Figures of Light who first received it. It is also the foundation of Shiite ethical life.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01724

Two familiar Persian terms express the principle: tawalla wa tabarra. One must take God's friends and the friends of those friends as one's own, and turn away from their enemies. From the very beginning, moreover, God's special love gives those whom he has loved from eternity a kind of claim (haqq) upon him.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01725

This explains a striking expression often used in Shiite prayers. It sounds almost like a final, irresistible appeal: by invoking the claim that God himself has granted his friends, the person praying seems to invoke a promise whose fulfilment is already assured. The Imams themselves used the words bi-haqqina: “by the right granted to us,” or “in the name of our cause.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01726

In some passages, this appeal to the Imams' “right” also answers Mufaddal's question. Because the right has its origin beyond historical time, prophets could invoke it long before the Imams appeared in their earthly lives. The way events become present together here may seem bewildering from the standpoint of ordinary history.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01727

Yet it is the key to sacred history. Again and again, invoking this right—appealing “in the name of this cause”—brings each prophet's earthly trial to its resolution. It is for the sake of this cause that God “turned again to Adam” after his exile from paradise. And because the same cause is the secret behind the Qur'anic account of Christ being saved from death and raised up by God (4:156), its invocation by the prophets rules out even the possibility of killing God.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01728

A tradition going back through the Eighth Imam, Ali Rida, to earlier Imams declares: “When Noah was in danger of drowning, he called upon God in the name of our cause [or our right], and God saved him from the waters. When Abraham was thrown into the fire, he called upon God in the name of our cause, and God made the fire cool and harmless.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01729

“When Moses opened a path through the sea, he called upon God in the name of our cause, and God turned the sea into dry ground. And when the Jews sought to kill Jesus, he called upon God in the name of our cause; so God saved him from death and raised him up to himself [Qur'an 4:156].”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01730

Another account, one among many, expresses the same idea: all the prophets belong to this single religion of walayat, and events that seem separated by centuries are joined at a deeper level. Here the Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir, speaks with his disciple Jabir al-Ju'fi. Their conversation belongs to a group of traditions offering Shiite interpretations of the Hebrew Bible. “I asked the Imam,” the disciple recalls, “whether Daniel's interpretation of dream visions was genuine. ‘Yes, it was genuine,’ he answered.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01731

“‘Daniel truly received a revelation from God, because he was a prophet (nabi). He was among those whom God taught the hidden meaning of events (ta'wil al-ahadith). He was truthful and wise. And the divine religion he followed was the religion of love for us—the Prophet's Household (Ahl al-Bayt).’” This makes sense only within the vision of the primordial Muhammadan Reality.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01732

Jabir does not yet see that. Surprised, he asks the same question that Mufaddal asked Ja'far: “Love for you? For the Prophet's Household?” The Imam replies: “Yes, by God! There has never been a prophet or an angel who did not follow the religion of love for us (illa wa kana yadinu bi-mahabbatina).”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01733

The meaning could hardly be clearer. We are speaking of a “religion of love,” and the speaker is not a Sufi master but the Fifth Shiite Imam. In this understanding, the followers of every prophet have always belonged to that religion, because love for the divine Face revealed to them was the hidden heart of every prophetic message.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01734

We have now reached the centre of our question. We have seen why walayat is understood as the enduring prophetic religion of humanity: “the Imam was sent secretly with each prophet.” We have also seen what the Imam means for sacred history—for the history of spiritual events that unfold in a kind of time different from the time of ordinary earthly history.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01735
We can now begin to grasp his meaning for Shiite spiritual life itself. Shiism's universal outlook rests on the belief that love for the divine Face reaches across all times and peoples.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01736

But to recognize this Face, each person must turn towards self-knowledge. Love is not simply added to faith; it is part of faith's very foundation. Through that love, Shiism sees all true believers as members of one enduring prophetic community, called to seek the Soul of their soul. The movement from the Imam's role in sacred history to his role in each person's innermost life is itself an example of the principle of Shiite interpretation that has guided our discussion throughout this book.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01737

The sacred Book remains alive throughout our present age because its inner meaning—the meaning of walayat—continues to unfold in every new believer. From one period of the prophetic cycle to another, sacred history preserves an underlying pattern. The same kinds of people return, both those who carry the message and those who resist it. Faith kindles the same enthusiasm, and the same active refusal rises against it.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01738

The names and the individual actors change, but the roles in the drama remain. This continuing pattern is expressed by the distinction between the prophets' missions, which come to an end, and walayat, which is eternal. It is also expressed in the relationship joining every prophet and every person of spiritual knowledge to the “Seal of the Prophets” and the “Seal of God's Friends.” Because walayat is the inward secret of the same message repeated from prophet to prophet until the final Prophet, it joins them and their followers in a single spiritual body, the corpus mysticum—the Temple of Light of the Imamate.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01739

But what does it mean to belong to that body? How does love of the Imam make a believer—someone “whose heart God has tested”—a member of this spiritual community, ultimately described as the Ahl al-Bayt, the members of the holy Family, the prophetic “house” or “temple”? And how, in the First Imam's own words, does the believer whose heart has been tested discover that love within himself?
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01740

We already know that, without the Imamate, the hidden God (Deus absconditus) could be approached only through a theology of negation—the way of tanzih, which Christian tradition calls apophatic or “negative” theology. Only through God's revealed Face, the form in which he appears (mazhar), can the hidden God become someone we can know and love: Deus revelatus, God as revealed.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01741

Yet to say that the Imam is this Face, this revealed form, is to say far more than something theoretical about God. It reaches directly into a believer's personal life. To accept it means entering into an actual relationship. And recognizing the Imam as the form through which God appears is, at the same time, the beginning of self-knowledge.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01742

When the believer comes to know himself in this way, he becomes a form through which the Imam is revealed, just as the Imam is the form through which the hidden God is revealed. This is why the Fifth Imam could say: “We are God's treasurers and God's treasures in this world and the next”—we shall return to the fuller meaning of this statement—“and our Shiites are our treasurers and our treasures.” The Imamate contains, as a treasure, divine knowledge. And in every Shiite believer whose heart has been tested, some part of the knowledge of the Imam comes to life.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01743

This theme is explored with remarkable depth in the writings of an important Iranian shaykh from the previous century, Hajj Muhammad Karim Khan Kermani (died 1870; see Book VI below). Unfortunately, I can give only the briefest account of his argument. In one chapter of a major work, he shows that love of God is realized through love of the Imams. More fundamentally still, there can be no love of God that is not, at the same time, love of them. The chapter develops a saying of the First Imam: “No person whose heart God has tested for faith has failed, in the end, to discover our love within that heart.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01744
What we most need to take from Kermani's demanding argument is a movement in two stages.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01745

First, all knowledge and love of God prove to be knowledge and love of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones—or simply of the Imam, whose person gathers their whole company into one. Second, as the believer lives out that relationship, knowledge of the Imam becomes knowledge of the believer's own self.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01746

1. We have said that the Imam gives human meaning to whatever human beings can know of God, whether through their own understanding or through divine revelation. As the one towards whom walayat is directed, the Imam also makes it possible for human beings to love God and gives that love its meaning. Muhammad Karim Khan Kermani examines this idea with exceptional care.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01747

At the deepest level of the divine essence (kunh al-dhat)—the reality beyond every essence, which philosophers call hyperousion and which may be compared with Meister Eckhart's Grund—God is absolutely one, utterly alone, pure, and undivided. Nothing can be said of this reality. No name or description applies to it; it resembles nothing, and nothing resembles it. As such, it cannot be the object of one particular being's love, nor can its love be directed towards one particular being.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01748

Love, after all, calls for some likeness or proportion between two beings, so that each can move towards the other and they can come together. The divine love that belongs to this highest, unknowable level—the love of the Hidden Treasure longing to be known—embraces everything that exists. It is what gives existence the weight that overcomes nonexistence. This is the meaning associated with the universal divine Will (mashiat amma kawniya), which is examined in the philosophy of existence.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01749

Theologians, however, have another task: to reflect on a particular divine Will (mashiat khassa shariya), a Will that relates to distinct beings and things, loving some and rejecting others in their particularity. The place in which divine Will becomes manifest (mahall), in both the philosophical and the religious sense, is formed by the primordial Figures of Light: the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. Many traditions of the Imams describe them in this way.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01750

Because they are where divine Will becomes manifest in both senses, their complete company forms the passage from what cannot be reached or described to what can be known and revealed. In a certain sense, then, they are that Will itself: the manifestation it wills to bring forth. They are God's Names, the bearers of attributes that cannot be ascribed to God's essence beyond all description. They are the ma'ani: the positive meanings through which the divine intentions are expressed in the Names and Attributes.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01751

In short, they are the forms in which God can be known by human beings—what Kermani calls God's knowability (marufiya). A person whose deepest life comes to resemble theirs becomes capable of entering into the relationship with God, “because the Fourteen Immaculate Ones are themselves that relationship.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01752

To love them is therefore to love God. They are not only the way in which God can be known, but also the way in which God can be loved—God's being an object of love (mahbubiya). And whoever is loved by them is loved by God, because they are God's own love, the way in which God is the one who loves (muhibbiya). Notice how well classical Arabic serves this sort of philosophical thought: from a word meaning “the one who acts” or “the one acted upon,” it can form an abstract noun naming the corresponding state or quality.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01753

A person who has come to share something of the Imams' spiritual nature, whose innermost life is shaped by their example and whose love for them reaches every part of his being, is drawn into union with their own souls—their very selves (bi-anfusihim). This is the complete and specially favoured believer (mu'min khasis kamil), who, like Salman the Persian, is taken into the holy Family (Ahl al-Bayt) in this world and the next.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01754

The Shiite believer is said to be “created from the rays of their light.” That light is the very substance of the believer's being. The form it takes depends on how fully the person is able to receive it. This gives rise to different degrees of spiritual life, as we saw earlier (III, §4). Only through this likeness can a human being love God. Without it, the absolute difference between God and humanity would rule out a relationship of love.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01755

God becomes knowable and lovable through the form in which God appears. In that revealed form, the lover, the beloved, and love itself are united. That form is the Imam. It safeguards the truth of divine oneness from both of the dangers we have examined. And here lies the secret of the Imam's life within every believer: he is the one who stands ahead of the believer's being, the centre from which everything begins and to which everything returns.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01756

2. It is precisely because the Imam lives within the spiritual life of the believer that he can lead the believer towards self-knowledge. As the highest object of knowledge and love, he reveals the Self that is the Soul of one's soul. Every Shiite—and indeed every human being—has a highest thought, a furthest limit of understanding. No one can pass beyond that limit without losing the very form of his or her own being.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01757
Yet the fact that this is our highest thought also tells us that something greater lies beyond it.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01758

We cannot reach that further reality by simply breaking through the limit of what we are. Kermani explains that reaching the highest point within our being—the reality that stands “ahead of our being”—is what it means to “reach ourselves.” This is the nafs: the self understood as soul or heart, the most personal centre of life, the Self that is the Soul of the soul.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01759

Hence the saying, “Whoever knows his own soul knows his God.” We are speaking, of course, about someone for whom this spiritual level has become a lasting state, not a momentary experience. At that highest point, what is otherwise beyond all reach becomes accessible in the only way it can. The person does not have to leave behind the limits of the self, make the transcendent God fit the self, or try to make the self fit an utterly transcendent God. Without the Imam, each of these attempts would endanger the very understanding of divine oneness it was meant to preserve.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01760

The relation between knowing ourselves, knowing the Imam, and knowing God becomes clearer through what we might call Kermani's account of the Highest (al-ali, what is above) and the lowest (al-dani, what is below). The Highest cannot descend as it is, in such a way that the lowest could directly perceive and understand it. The absolute difference between them would remain, still making knowledge and love impossible. Nor can the Highest descend by changing its own essence, giving up its true nature so that it becomes like the lowest.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01761
But there is another possibility. Kermani writes:
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01762

If this descent takes place not by altering or emptying the Highest of its nature, but through a manifestation of God (tajalli), an appearance (zuhur), an attribute (sifat), a Light (nur), then we have found what we are looking for. For if this manifestation did not correspond to the faculties through which Shiite believers perceive (masha'ir), we would still face the same problem.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01763
But if it does correspond to them, the manifestation has something in common with the believers. It belongs to their own being, and they can reach it.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01764
What is present in the manifestation is also present within them. Otherwise, it would make no sense to require them to reach it.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01765

So the Highest makes itself known to the lowest through an attribute that the lowest can perceive, know, and understand. This is the highest level the lowest can reach, the furthest point of its thought. It is its own soul—its self (nafs)—and its heart. As the tradition says: “Whoever knows himself, his own soul, knows his Lord.” The Qur'an points towards the same truth: “And within yourselves are signs. Do you not see?” (51:21). And again: “We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within their souls”—that is, within themselves (41:53).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01766

In this way, God makes himself known to Shiite believers through their own selves, their own souls. When they come to know themselves, they have fulfilled what is asked of them: they have reached the one who stands ahead of their being, their Imam [...]. They are manifestations of their Imam, just as the Imams are the manifestation and meaning of God. It is of them that the Ziyarat al-Jami'a says (see Chapter V above): “Peace be upon those whom, if you know them, you know God, and if you do not know them, you do not know God.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01767

Kermani's words, together with our discussion so far, lead to a clear conclusion. The Imam is the form in which God becomes manifest (mazhar). Through that form, God can be known and loved. To reach it is to reach knowledge of God, because it is the only form in which God can be known.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01768

For the human being, it is therefore the highest possible level of existence, understanding, and love. Every manifestation of God creates a relationship between the one who reveals himself (mutajalli) and the one to whom he appears (mutajalla lahu). What appears must take a form suited to the person receiving it. Ibn Arabi had already insisted on this point.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01769
But here the relationship is understood specifically through the teaching about the Imam. It is this teaching that makes the relationship possible without compromising God's oneness.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01770

A manifestation of God (tajalli) is possible because the form in which God appears has something in common with the person who receives it. And because that manifestation is the highest reality that a person living in this lower world can reach, to arrive at its “place”—the believer's own mystical Mount Sinai—is to reach the summit, or the deepest centre, of one's being: the self, the soul (nafs). The form in which God appears there, the Face revealed at the summit of the soul, is the Imam. This is why knowing oneself, knowing one's soul and all that belongs to its world, means knowing one's Imam. And for each person, that is what knowing the Lord means.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01771

The Imam is the form taken by the revealed God (Deus revelatus) when self-knowledge becomes knowledge of God. The Imam is the form through which I know and love God. When a believer comes to know the Imam, this knowledge reveals itself as the very form of the believer's love—and therefore as the secret of the believer's existence, because that existence is itself an act of love. That is why love of the Imam, the religion of walayat, is also an initiation into self-knowledge.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01772

In the Shiite understanding, it embraces the whole of an eternal prophetic religion and the followers of every prophet. The Self it reveals is not an empty, impersonal Absolute. It is the Soul and Beloved of the soul (jan-e jan): a “you” at the centre of my “I,” the one who “walks ahead of me.” This is the Imam, in the original meaning of the word itself.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01773

Shiite devotion and spiritual life thus reach their fullest expression in walayat, love directed towards the Imam as the form through which the hidden God reveals himself. It is through this form that the hidden God becomes someone who can be loved—God's lovability (mahbubiya). In that sense, every love of God, simply because it is love directed towards a God who can be loved, is walayat towards the Imam. Sufis outside Shiism struggled to find such a way forward, longing to escape what Ruzbihan calls the “madness of the unreachable.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01774

What matters here is that Shiism itself has already asked the question and answered it through the teaching about the Imam. This is the meaning of the many titles given to the Imam in Shiite prayers. The titles echo those the Imams use for themselves in their sayings: Guide, Pole, A'raf, Witness of God, and others. Each points back to the same central insight. To know oneself is to know the Imam; and knowing the Imam is knowing God, because no other knowledge of God is available to human beings.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01775

We can explore only the titles I have just mentioned. To bring this account of Shiite spiritual life to a close, I want to show how they were understood by thinkers for whom philosophical reflection could never be separated from personal spiritual practice and experience. Above all, I shall turn again to Mulla Sadra Shirazi, whose work we have encountered so often already.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01776

Along with Saleh Mazandarani, Mohsen Fayz, Qazi Sa'id Qummi, and others, Mulla Sadra belongs to a group of Shiite thinkers who produced immense works of commentary on the sayings of the Imams. Their writings help explain why their philosophy is sometimes called “prophetic and Imamic wisdom” (hikmat nabawiya wa walawiya, the second adjective coming from wali). At other times they call it “Yemeni divine wisdom” (hikmat yamaniya), a reference to the symbolic meaning of Yemen and the Yemeni corner of the Kaaba. The expression also recalls a saying that plays on the similar sounds of iman, meaning faith, and Yaman, meaning Yemen: “Faith comes from Yemen, and wisdom—divine wisdom—is Yemeni.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01777

“Yemeni divine wisdom” and “Eastern divine wisdom”—the Illuminationist teaching (Ishraq) of Suhrawardi, an especially Iranian and Islamic form of Neoplatonism—draw their strength from the same sources. Both look to the traditions of walayat and to the Imam as a Figure of Light, the Face of God who reveals himself only by remaining veiled. From this comes the understanding of the Imam as the Witness of God. At the highest point of the believer's soul, the Imam is the believer's living awareness of God—the witness within who bears witness to a God otherwise beyond all reach.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01778

In Mulla Sadra's work, to which we shall return particularly in these final pages, this becomes a philosophy of the witness and the act of witnessing. The person who contemplates and the reality contemplated become one. Existence itself is understood through presence: the soul's growing presence in more and more worlds. As it becomes present to those worlds, it is freed from confinement to this mortal world.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01779

The understanding of the Imam as part of spiritual experience undoubtedly shaped Mulla Sadra's philosophy of existence. Rather than giving first place to the fixed natures of things, as older philosophy often did, he gives priority to existing itself (see Book V below).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01780

But the journey towards self-knowledge requires the possibility of a transformation that reaches into the very substance of a being. Mulla Sadra calls this “substantial movement” (harakat jawhariya), and it is fundamental to his philosophy. It is also the key to the Mabda' and the Ma'ad—the beginning and the return—which open the possibility of sensing transformations that took place before we can remember, and future renewals of our existence. The two “arcs,” one of descent and one of return, enclose a vision of existence far wider than what the West has usually meant by evolution.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
en-book-1-ch-7-s2
2. The Imam as Guide and Spiritual Centre
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01781

Everything we have discussed so far has brought this central idea of prophetic philosophy into view. Here, we need only bring its essential points together. The first is the question we have put so directly: what happens after the Prophet is gone, when there will be no further prophet? The true meaning of his revelation cannot be found in the outward words alone.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01782

Nor can anyone arrive at it simply by constructing an argument or drawing a series of conclusions. It can be revealed and passed on only by someone who knows. The Shiite traditions answer this question by joining the Imam and the Qur'an into a single, inseparable reality: the Qur'an is the silent Imam, and the Imam is the speaking Qur'an.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01783

As the speaking Qur'an, the Imam is the guide who is always present: the one who leads people into the true meaning of Qur'anic revelation and keeps the Book alive as God's living word. We have already discussed sayings of the Fifth Imam that anticipate and overcome the danger of reducing revelation to the history of the time in which it appeared. The Sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq, makes the same point when he tests one of his disciples. “Abu Muhammad,” he asks, “the Prophet was the Warner, and Ali was the Guide.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01784

“But is there a Guide (hadi) today?” His disciple replies, “Yes, may my life be given for yours! In your family, one guide has always followed another, down to you.” The Imam answers, “May God have mercy on you, Abu Muhammad! If a verse revealed on the occasion of a particular person's life were to die when that person died, the entire Book would be dead by now.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01785
“But no! The Qur'an is alive. It will continue to find its fulfilment among people in the future, just as it did among those who lived in the past.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01786

The meaning could hardly be clearer. If we could understand the sacred Book only by relating it to “its own time,” to the social and historical circumstances in which its verses first appeared, the Qur'an would have been dead for centuries. Without the continuing walayat—the spiritual bond and authority of God's Friends—in this world, the Book of God would have no future. The life of the Imam and the life of the sacred Book depend on each other.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01787

The Imam and his companions must therefore remain present in the world. This was the subject of the First Imam's conversation with Komayl ibn Ziyad, quoted above (III, 3). We had already encountered the idea of a spiritual centre, or pole, without which the human world itself could not endure. Mulla Sadra echoes the First Imam when he writes: “The Earth can never be without an Imam, a guide for every age. Otherwise the Qur'an would have to die when those who sustain it die.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01788
“But the Qur'an is alive and will never die before the Day of Resurrection. At every moment, until the final Hour, someone living guides people towards it.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01789

This is precisely what we find throughout the sayings collected in the chapter of Kolayni's great work devoted to the Imam as Guide and as God's witness and guarantor (Hojjat): the one who speaks for God before humanity. We should remember some of these sayings, in which the Imams show their unwavering awareness of who they are. The Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir, declares: “God is my witness!
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01790

“From the moment Adam's soul was taken—that is, from Adam's death—God has never allowed an earthly world to exist without an Imam to guide people towards Him. That Imam is God's witness before His servants, and the world is never left without an Imam who stands before humanity as that witness and guide.” The Tenth Imam, Ali Naqi, says: “Truly, the earthly world is never without a witness and guide. And God is my witness: at this moment, I am that person.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01791

Abu Hamza, a disciple of the Sixth Imam, recalls: “I asked Imam Ja'far, ‘Can the Earth remain without an Imam?’ He answered, ‘If the Earth were left without an Imam, it would sink away.’” The Fifth Imam also says: “If the Imam were taken away from the Earth for even an hour, the Earth would heave in waves, tossing its inhabitants as the sea tosses the creatures living within it.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01792
These declarations suggest a mysterious bond—almost a sacred bond—between the Imam's presence and the continuing existence of the human world. Several consequences follow.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01793

First, the need for an Imam is plainly not just another political or social question. It concerns the unseen order and structure of reality itself. The Imam is the spiritual Pole, the Pole of poles (qotb al-aqtab), the centre on which the world depends.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01794

Mulla Sadra explains this in a particularly dense passage. The need for an Imam expresses an inner law of existence: every higher level of being is the goal towards which the level below it moves. The lower level exists through the higher one, and can reach fulfilment only in it. The lower level therefore presupposes the higher; the reverse is not true. This is more than a law of development. It is a movement upwards towards a higher kind of being that already exists.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01795

Humanity follows the same pattern. It can reach fulfilment only at the highest level of human perfection. This is what the Imamate means. “The degree of the Imamate,” Mulla Sadra explains, “means the Perfect Human Being (al-insan al-kamil, anthropos teleios), who is the king of the earthly world.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01796

But this kingship belongs to the Perfect Human Being as the very goal of existence. It does not arise from political circumstances, or depend on them. To treat the Imam simply as a rival to the Umayyads or Abbasids would place him on the wrong level altogether. We are dealing with something that social history alone cannot describe: a form of kingship that does not, by its nature, require political success in this world. Still less does it depend on the claim that majorities are always right because they are the ones who “make” history.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01797
Another history is unfolding without their knowing it. It is the history of a hidden spiritual kingship over the visible world—something like the role played by the guardians of the Grail.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01798

Other consequences follow immediately. As we have seen, the idea that the Imam might remain unknown was already present in the Prophet's declarations limiting the Imams of his own line to twelve. With a fixed number of Imams, the Imamate must eventually enter a state of concealment (ghaybat). The Shiite believer's present relationship with the Imam, as the spiritual centre of their own being, is therefore not a relationship with an institution in this world. It is a relationship with a world beyond what the physical senses can perceive. The Twelfth Imam appeared briefly in the earthly world, but his continuing presence is now invisible.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01799

This means that his mode of existence transcends the ordinary biological conditions of earthly life. Such a presence can be experienced only in visions or through encounters in which his identity remains hidden.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01800

Yet this invisible presence lies at the centre of Shiite devotion. Ordinary believers and scholars alike live in a sense of familiarity with the Imam (see Book Seven below). He need not be visible to the physical eye, any more than he needs to be known or recognised by the masses or by worldly rulers.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01801

Being an Imam is intrinsic to what he is: the Perfect Human Being. Human ignorance or blindness cannot take that away from him. Here we reach the fundamental difference between the Shiite understanding of the Imam as guide and spiritual centre and the Sunni understanding of the Imam. The two concepts cannot be reduced to one another.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01802

We have already stressed this difference when discussing Mulla Sadra's treatment of a long account of the Imam by the Sunni theologian and philosopher Fakhr al-Din Razi. In the Shiite understanding, the Imam is the centre on which the coherence and unity of existence depend. His presence is necessary at the deepest level of reality. His task is to lead people into spiritual knowledge, and it opens towards the events of the last days, when the Twelfth Imam is to appear as the Mahdi. His role and its necessity belong to what he is. They do not change according to whether people recognise him.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01803

In the Sunni account discussed here, by contrast, the Imam is the centre of social order, and there is no need to appeal to the hidden structure of reality to explain his role. He is necessary because of the requirements of life in this world. The concept is not sacred in the sense of giving the universe a sacred structure; it belongs to public and political life.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01804

Neither the Imam's person nor his office requires the kind of spiritual necessity or end-time role found in the Shiite account. Consequently, this view does not require him to know the ta'wil, the inner meanings of the Qur'an; to possess knowledge inspired directly by God (ilm laduni); or to be protected from every impurity and failure (isma). Choosing him is therefore a matter of agreement among people: he is elected.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01805

The Shiite reply is that people can elect a political leader or president, or appoint someone to religious office, but it makes no sense to speak of electing a prophet or an Imam. Their special calling is not created by human choice. More than that, most people cannot even perceive the quality that makes them what they are.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01806

As the saying puts it: “My Friends (awliya'i) are hidden beneath My tents; no one knows them but Me.” And consider the saying we have just seen at the heart of Shiite spirituality: “Whoever dies without knowing the Imam of their time dies the death of those who know nothing.” To apply that saying to the Sunni idea of the Imam described here would not merely empty it of meaning. It would make it monstrous.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01807

This brings us to an objection Sunnis have often raised against Shiites, and to the Shiite answer. The objection runs as follows: “You say the Imam is necessary because God has made him necessary. In that case his rule should never be interrupted; there should be no concealment (ghaybat).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01808
“But you also call him a gift of divine grace. Either he is necessary, in which case he is not a gift of grace, or he is a gift of grace, in which case he is not necessary.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01809

The Shiite response is: “The Imam's existence remains a gift of divine grace, whether he exercises political power or not. As the Commander of the Faithful [the First Imam] said: ‘The earthly world is never left without someone who speaks for God, whether openly and with public recognition, or secretly and unknown to others.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01810

“Otherwise the signs of God and His manifestation would disappear from the Earth.’ The Imam's freedom to exercise outward rule would be another gift of grace. The prophetic mission that brought religious law has reached its end and been sealed; but the Imamate, which is the inner meaning of prophecy, endures until the Day of Resurrection. This remains true whether people recognise the Imam or reject him.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01811

“A messenger of God is still a messenger even if no one believes his message, as happened, for example, with Noah. In the same way, the Imam remains an Imam even if no human being recognises him. A doctor does not cease to be a doctor simply because no patient comes seeking treatment or healing. The same is true of the doctors of the soul, who treat spiritual sickness and the afflictions of the heart: the prophets and God's Friends.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01812

The answer is unmistakable: the Imam remains the Imam under all circumstances, even when he must carry out his mission in secret. Public opinion, official recognition, or the absence of recognition tells us nothing about whether his presence is necessary. The Imamate and the prophetic mission form a single reality in their deepest nature (haqiqat wahida bi'l-dhat).
